1:
Who the messenger was is the question of the passage, and four of them answer it the same way against the Jewish tradition. Gill reports that the Targum calls him a prophet and the Jewish commentators generally make him Phinehas, others agreeing a man is meant because he comes from a place in Canaan rather than from heaven and is not said to disappear; but he rejects it on one ground, that a man or a created angel would have said, thus saith the Lord, whereas this speaker ascribes to himself the bringing of Israel out of Egypt, the oath to the fathers and the covenant. Henry adds that the Old Testament prophets are never called angels of the Lord, cites a bishop for the Angel of the covenant and a Hebraist for Christ himself, and asks who but God could say, I made you to go up out of Egypt. Keil reaches the same conclusion from the sacrifice offered at Bochim where there was no sanctuary, which follows only if the person who appeared was neither a prophet nor an ordinary angel. Ellicott states the strongest objection, that in no other instance does an angel preach to multitudes, angels being sent to individuals and prophets to nations, but answers it by supposing the Angel Prince of the host left his station in the camp at Gilgal and came up to the new assembly.

The place and the text both raise smaller questions. Ellicott notes that the Greek adds to Bethel and to the house of Israel, from which some infer that Bochim was near Bethel, though he suspects the translators were led there by the neighbouring oak of weeping; and he reports a conjecture that words have dropped out at the opening, since some manuscripts leave a blank there as if the formula thus saith the Lord had fallen away. On the threat he observes that the Hebrew says only they shall be to you for sides, the words as thorns being supplied by conjecture from Numbers, and canvasses three readings without thinking the sense affected. Henry says the coming from Gilgal was to remind them of the favours received there and of the renewal of the covenant; he adds that Joshua had lately given the same warning and they had disregarded a dying man, so the living God brings it himself. On the sacrifice both Keil and Ellicott deny that it proves a sanctuary there, since sacrifice was freely offered wherever there had been a manifestation of the divine presence, though Ellicott adds that it is improbable all Israel assembled at a wholly unknown spot.

The weeping is weighed rather than admired. Keil takes it for grief on account of sin, leading on to such repentance that they sacrificed, presenting offerings that they might obtain mercy. Henry divides it, that they wept in confession of the sins charged and in dread of the judgments threatened, and that it was a sign the word had made an impression, since it is a wonder sinners can ever read their Bible with dry eyes; but he will not call it enough, for we do not find that they reformed or destroyed what remained of idolatry among them, and many are melted under the word who harden again before they are cast into a new mould. Had they kept close to God, he adds, no voice but singing would have been heard in their assembly, whereas by their own folly they made other work and nothing is heard but the voice of weeping. Clarke stands back and treats this chapter with the first verses of the next as an epitome of the whole book, in which we see on one hand the crimes of the Israelites and on the other the punishments inflicted, their repentance and return, and the long-suffering of God in pardoning their backslidings.
6:
The paragraph looks backward, and they explain why. Gill insists it is not to be connected with what precedes as though the dismissal happened in Joshua's lifetime, since during that time Israel served the Lord, whereas the angel charges them with disobedience and leagues and standing altars, all of which came after Joshua's death; the passage is repeated here to connect the history and to show how they fell into idolatry and so into distress. Keil says the same about the connection, that the verb expresses the order of thought and not of time, and that the closing verses of Joshua are repeated not merely to link the two books but to bring out sharply the contrast between the age that was past and the period now beginning. Henry adds the narrative reason: the angel had foretold that the Canaanites and their idols would be a snare, and the historian now undertakes to show that they were, looking back a little to do it. Clarke gives the whole in one summary, that the people continued faithful during Joshua's life and the lives of those who survived him, and that when all who had seen the wondrous works had died the succeeding generation forsook God for the gods of the nations among whom they lived.

The name of the burial place is disputed and the dispute has a history. Ellicott calls the form used here a mere slip of the pen, an accidental transposition of letters for the form found in Joshua, which is the reading of the best versions and of some manuscripts in this place too; but he grants the mistake is ancient, since it originated the rabbinic story that the name refers to the sun standing still and that an image of the sun was sculptured on the tomb. Henry reports the same story from the Jewish writers and doubts it on other grounds, that an image of the sun would hardly have been allowed to the honour of Joshua at a time when men were so generally prone to worship the sun that it would be in danger of being abused to the dishonour of God. Ellicott adds several details around the grave: that the Greek preserves a tradition that the flint knives of the neglected circumcision were buried in the tomb; that the district was rugged and barren, so that a later pilgrim was astonished the distributor of possessions had chosen rough mountain country for himself; that the name of the hill means mount earthquake; and that the age of a hundred and ten was the same as Joseph's.

The new generation is where the chapter turns. Ellicott glosses the phrase from the prophet, that they proceed from evil to evil and know not me, saith the Lord, and notes the several idioms for dying used in the verse. Henry presses it harder: they had every advantage of education, yet one might truly say they knew not the Lord, knew him not aright, knew him not as he had revealed himself, or they would not have forsaken him; they were so devoted to the world and so indulgent of the flesh that they never minded the true God, and so were easily drawn to false gods. He fixes the cause on what died with the elders, that the people persisted in their good resolutions as long as they had good rulers who set them examples and restrained the corruptions creeping in, and as long as the great things God had done were fresh in memory, for those who had seen them had sense enough to believe their own eyes, whereas those who followed, because they had not seen, believed not. Gill and Clarke both make the same connection more briefly, that the fathers had seen the works and the children had not.
11:
What the plural names mean is set out at length. Clarke explains that the word rendered Baalim signifies lords, the false gods being considered rulers each with his own district and office, so that a particular one was named by an added epithet, and he lists several with the peoples that adored them; where the word stands without an epithet, he says, the sun is probably meant. Ellicott adds that the definite article should be kept in both places, the evil and the Baalim, that the term was applied especially to the sun worshipped as the great nature power under a multitude of names, that the worship was plainly Phoenician, and that traces of it survive in the Carthaginian names compounded with it. He notes the attraction of a worship at once splendid and orgiastic to backsliding Israel, and reports the caution in Hosea against the too facile use of the word, where the Lord promises that his people shall call him my husband and no more my lord. On the female name he says the plural may be a plural of excellence or an allusion to the different forms under which the goddess was worshipped, identifies her with the Phoenician Venus, sometimes with the moon and sometimes with the planet, and warns against confusing her name with another which the English renders groves. Keil takes the same line, that the male deities of all these nations were in their nature one and the same sun-god, the source of the generative power of nature, while the female was a moon-goddess. Clarke says more briefly that the two probably mean the sun and moon, and that the goddess was worshipped with obscene rites.

Ellicott then offers a reading of the apostasy which the others do not. He judges that the sin of the Israelites was a breach rather of the second commandment than of the first, not so much a worshipping of other gods as a worshipping of the Lord under false symbols adopted from the surrounding nations by a spurious syncretism, and compares the calf-worship of the northern tribes, which was originally intended as an adoration of Jehovah under cherubic symbols and lapsed with dangerous facility into actual Baal-worship. Gill, Clarke and Keil read it plainly as forsaking the Lord for other gods, Gill noting that the repetition marks how heinous the sin was and how displeasing to God, and Clarke fixing on the aggravation, that they forsook the God who had brought them out of a place of the most grievous oppression by a display of power that should never have been forgotten, and served idols as destitute of real being as of influence.

The judgment is described in the terms of the covenant. Keil observes that the word for selling occurs in Deuteronomy in the sense of giving helplessly up to the foe, and that instead of the promise in Leviticus that five should chase a hundred, the threat in the same chapter was now carried into execution; Ellicott makes the same reference and sets the hand of the Lord against them beside the promise given to Joshua that the Lord would be with him. Clarke puts it in a sentence, that the power which before protected them was now turned against them, so that they not only had not God with them but had God against them, and he takes the spoilers for marauding parties making incursions, carrying off cattle and spoiling the crops. Gill reports that the Jewish expositors he names refer the going out to military expeditions and the battle going against them, though he notes that others in the Jewish writings apply it instead to those who went out of the land to escape its calamities, and name Elimelech and his two sons.
16:
Gill takes the opening word as marking a wonderful instance of the goodness of God notwithstanding their provoking sins: he raised up in an extraordinary manner men whom he spirited and qualified for the work of delivering Israel out of the hand of their oppressors, restoring their liberties and administering justice among them; these are the men whose exploits the following chapters record, and from whom the book takes its name. Clarke describes them as leaders, generals and governors raised up by an especial appointment of the Lord to deliver Israel from their adversaries and avenge them. Ellicott calls the verse the key-note of the whole book, would render its opening word simply and rather than nevertheless, and observes that the title is not formed from the ordinary Hebrew verb for judging, that these deliverers stood higher than the tribe-magistrates of the law, and that among the ancients to judge signified to govern. They took no salary, imposed no tribute and made no laws, exercising for the deliverance of Israel only the personal ascendency conferred upon them by the Spirit of God, and Ellicott finds their nearest analogies in the elective princes of the Greeks and in the Roman dictators. The disorder of the age, he adds, shows in the judges themselves: one the son of a stranger, another a woman, and not one of them of priestly or splendid birth.

On the next verse Gill remarks that when the judges admonished them of their sins and advised them to walk in the good ways of God they turned a deaf ear, which is a sad aggravation of their iniquity. On the figure of whoredom Clarke and Ellicott part slightly. Ellicott treats it as the spiritual adultery under which idolatry is described throughout the Bible, and takes the way their fathers walked in as the obedience of the elders described earlier. Clarke, granting the metaphor, holds that because many idolatrous practices were accompanied with impure rites the term was not only metaphorically but literally proper.

Gill notes that the Lord was with every one of the judges he raised, stirring up their spirits, assisting and strengthening them and succeeding whatever they engaged in for the welfare of the people, and reports the careful phrase of the Targum, that the Word of the Lord was for the help of the judge. Keil reads the deliverance as lasting exactly so long as the judge was living, grounded in the compassion of the Lord upon their sighing by reason of those who oppressed and vexed them. On the repenting of the Lord the other two take different roads. Clarke, holding that God himself was king and the judge his representative, explains it as a change of purpose and not of mind: the purpose was to destroy them if they did not repent, and when they did repent the sparing of them was quite consistent with it. Ellicott instead calls it the simple anthropomorphism of early ages, which never hesitates to describe the ways and thoughts of God by the analogy of human lives, and which the sacred writers qualified whenever they spoke in calm and unmetaphorical instruction, saying that God is not a man that he should repent, and that he changes not.

Clarke gathers from the last verse that the office of judge was in general for life, and renders their stubborn way as their hard or difficult way. Ellicott gives the literal sense of the clause about their doings, that they let nothing fall of them, and connects the word stubborn with the stiff-necked of the law and of the speech of Stephen. He adds that the prophets are always careful to impress upon Israel that they were chosen by the free grace of God to work out his purpose, and not for any merits of their own.
20:
Gill reads the kindling of the anger of the Lord here as no new thing but the same that had burned at the first, renewed whenever they fell into idolatry. Clarke puts it as a figure: they were the fuel, heaped up by their transgressions, and the displeasure of the Lord was as a fire about to kindle and consume it. Ellicott notes only that the phrase this people carries the same distancing force as in the commission of Isaiah, and that the charge of transgressing my covenant is worded as in the last address of Joshua.

Gill is careful with the sentence that follows, taking the refusal to drive out the nations as not absolute but a matter of delay, not as yet, not very soon nor hastily. Keil treats the whole as a formal resolution thrown into the shape of a divine utterance, and understands the covenant promise of the driving out of the nations to be suspended because the covenant has been broken on the other side. Clarke turns to Israel rather than to the nations. As a people, he says, they never had the personal courage, discipline or hardihood to stand before their enemies; every advantage they gained came by the peculiar interference of God, which lasted while they obeyed; when they ceased to obey his strong arm was no longer stretched out, and their enemies kept possession of the land intended for their inheritance.

On the proving of Israel Gill offers two senses. The Canaanites were an affliction by which their faith and patience were tried, as afflictions and temptations try the spiritual Israel of God; or rather, and this he prefers, the trial was whether they would keep in the ways of God or walk in the ways of the nations. Clarke agrees that there appeared to be no other way to bring this people to acknowledge the true God than to let them fall into straits out of which nothing but an especial providence could deliver them, and adds that the words are spoken after the manner of men. Ellicott insists that here as in all the punishments of God there was an element of mercy mingled with the judgment. Out of the evils that came of not exterminating Canaan at once God raised a two-fold good: Israel meanwhile grew numerous enough to till the soil and keep down the wild beasts, and was trained in bravery and warlike skill while the older inhabitants were driven out by little and little.

Gill returns at the close to the same two readings, that the nations were left either so that it might be seen whether Israel would give in to their idolatry, of which there could have been no trial had the idols been destroyed with their owners, or else as the penalty of the covenant already transgressed; both senses will stand, he judges, though the first agrees better with what follows. Keil fastens on the word hastily, which he finds strange after the flat refusal of the previous verse, and takes it to limit the threat: the Lord would exterminate no more of these nations so long as Israel persisted in its idolatry, but whenever Israel returned in true repentance to keep his covenant he would recall the threat and let the promised extermination go forward again. Clarke argues the same providence from the other end. Had the whole population been expelled at once, the people would soon have abandoned the worship of their deliverer and forgotten him in their prosperity; as it was, room enough was cleared for them as they then were, the land was kept from running to waste and the wild beasts from multiplying, and each rebellion brought its disaster and each humiliation its interposition, so that the whole history became a continual proof of the being, providence and grace of God.
